title: Redwood Structured Output & Function Calling Demo
summary: AE + SE walkthrough of Redwood structured output / function-calling features in the API and Console. Demonstrated JSON mode with schema enforcement, guardrails for hallucination reduction, and a sample integration for patient-summary generation. Discussed security (KMS, VPC), performance tradeoffs, and next steps: share security pack, run a short POC, and schedule benchmark run with sample data.
transcript:
[00:00] Avery Chen: Hi everyone, thanks for joining, this is Avery from Redwood, with Diego from engineering.
[00:06] Sofia Patel: Hey thanks, sorry for the delay, had back-to-back. We have about 40 minutes, right?
[00:12] Avery Chen: Yup, we planned 38 minutes, we'll show the Console demo then go into function calling and a short Q&A. Diego, you want to kick off?
[00:18] Diego Morales: Sure, thanks. So first quick context, this call is focused on JSON mode — structured outputs — and our function/tool calling. We'll show the API, the Console UI in Optimize and Console, and a small end-to-end example for patient-summary generation.
[00:30] Maya Reed: Great, our product team is especially interested in schemas and guardrails — we can't have hallucinated diagnoses.
[00:36] Diego Morales: Absolutely, that's the core. We'll show how schema validation plus a light wrapper that does semantic checks reduces risks.
[00:44] Liam O'Connor: Quick note: we run in a VPC and need KMS for keys — can you handle that in Private?
[00:50] Avery Chen: Yes, Private supports customer-managed KMS and HSM integrations. We'll share the security pack after this.
[00:58] Diego Morales: Ok jumping to the Console — I'm sharing my screen now — apologies if the slides load slow.
[01:06] [screen share noise]
[01:12] Diego Morales: Here's the API section. We have a JSON mode toggle — when on, you can supply a JSON Schema that the model must follow. I have an example schema for a patient_summary: fields like patient_id, age, diagnoses (array), recommended_actions (array of objects with type and urgency).
[01:30] Maya Reed: Is the schema enforced strictly or softly?
[01:34] Diego Morales: Good question. We support two enforcement modes: 'soft' where we bias the model to produce schema-compliant output using constrained decoding + post-parse correction, and 'strict' which will reject outputs that don't match — that triggers a fallback or retry. Strict mode is useful when you need exact JSON for downstream systems.
[01:52] Sofia Patel: If it rejects, does it count as an error in our app or do you return a sanitized fallback?
[01:58] Diego Morales: You can configure fallback routes — e.g., retry with a higher temperature/structured prompt, or route to a simpler deterministic template. We'll show an example of automatic fallback to a cached template.
[02:08] [typing sounds]
[02:14] Diego Morales: Now I'll run a live API call — I'm switching to the code snippet. This is the cURL request: model:redwood-alpha-1, mode:json, schema: patient_summary_schema.json, function_call: patient_summary_webhook.
[02:28] Liam O'Connor: Are functions hosted by you or are they just a call descriptor? We want functions to call our internal webhook behind the VPC.
[02:34] Diego Morales: Functions are descriptors only — the model returns a structured payload indicating which function to call and with what args. You host the webhook in your VPC. For Private customers we can set up secure routing or a sidecar to deliver the payload.
[02:48] Avery Chen: Important to note: Redwood doesn't execute your code. We produce a JSON object and metadata like confidence and token-level alignment scores so you can decide to call or not.
[02:58] Maya Reed: Ah okay that helps. Show us the output?
[03:02] Diego Morales: Here's the first run — it produced a JSON that matched schema except one missing field in recommended_actions. Because we're in soft mode it returned with a warning tag: {"_schema_ok": false, "issues": ["recommended_actions[0].urgency missing"]} and the payload.
[03:18] Sofia Patel: Hmm, how often does that happen in practice? We need >99% pass for downstream ingestion.
[03:24] Diego Morales: In our benchmarks, with tuned prompts and the right quantization profile, we see >97% schema compliance on noisy clinical notes; strict mode raises that but increases latency and occasional rejections. Our Optimize tool suggests a config for your workload.
[03:38] [short pause]
[03:44] Diego Morales: Let me show guardrails — we have a 'facts check' pipeline that runs post-generation against a retriever of structured records; it marks statements as verified/unsupported. This is pluggable and you can provide your own patient DB.
[03:56] Liam O'Connor: So we could reject any generated diagnosis not in the patient's record?
[03:59] Diego Morales: Exactly. You can set policy rules: reject, flag, or add a provenance note.
[04:06] Maya Reed: Can we map severity levels to internal taxonomy?
[04:10] Diego Morales: Yes, mapping layers are supported — you provide a mapping table and the post-processor will normalize strings.
[04:16] [crosstalk]
[04:20] Avery Chen: Quick pause for timeline/decision: Sofia, you mentioned an internal POC window?
[04:24] Sofia Patel: We want to evaluate this by end of Q4 — a 2-week POC ingesting ~5k anonymized notes.
[04:30] Avery Chen: Perfect, that's doable. We'll propose a Dedicated slot with private networking for the POC.
[04:36] Diego Morales: Back to the demo — I'm toggling strict mode now. This run will reject non-conforming JSON and return an error code + structured diagnostics.
[04:48] [typing]
[04:52] Diego Morales: Example response: {"error":"schema_mismatch","diagnostics":["missing recommended_actions[0].urgency"]}. We then automatically kick a retry with expanded prompt context and we show the retry trace in the Console.
[05:08] Maya Reed: What's the latency implication?
[05:11] Diego Morales: Soft mode single-pass median latency is lower. Strict with retries can add 200-700 ms per retry depending on model and sequence length; on Dedicated with batching tuned it's negligible for throughput but affects p99 latency. Optimize gives you recommendations: smaller context window, prefix caching, or using the 'fast-structured' kernel we have for JSON templates.
[05:32] Sofia Patel: Can you quantify cost diff between soft and strict?
[05:36] Avery Chen: Generally strict costs ~10-30% more due to retries and extra tokens; Optimize will show token-level cost and suggest quantization and batching to offset it. We'll share a sample cost sheet.
[05:48] Diego Morales: Now function calling: I'm going to show a demonstration where the model picks the patient_summary_webhook function and returns args as JSON. Watch the 'function_call' field and the confidence meta.
[05:58] [demo audio lag]
[06:02] Diego Morales: Ok payload returned. Note the model added a provenance note: source_passages: [record_id:1234 snippet: "patient had chest pain..."], and a token_confidence array.
[06:14] Liam O'Connor: Token-level confidence — how reliable is that?
[06:18] Diego Morales: It's an internal heuristic based on attention and logit gap; not absolute but useful for scoring. For clinical infra, we recommend combining it with deterministic checks.
[06:28] Maya Reed: Let's talk about hosting: if we run Private in our VPC, do we still get Console traces and Optimize suggestions?
[06:36] Avery Chen: Yes, Private ships a control plane that collects telemetry you opt in to, with RBAC and SSO. For air-gapped customers we provide an on-prem bundle for visibility and offline analytics.
[06:46] Sofia Patel: Audit logs are a must for us.
[06:48] Avery Chen: We provide immutable audit logs and can forward them to your SIEM. SOC2 and ISO options are documented in the security pack.
[06:56] [short pause]
[07:00] Diego Morales: I'm going to switch to the Optimize tab now — this is where we run batch evals and get suggestions. For your two-week POC we'd run a small eval harness against sample notes and provide recommendations: model variant, quantization profile, batch size, cache TTL.
[07:18] Liam O'Connor: Who runs the evals — you or us?
[07:21] Diego Morales: We can run them if you provide anonymized samples; or we provide a self-serve script that your infra team runs. Both work.
[07:30] Maya Reed: Can Optimize detect hallucination trends over time?
[07:34] Diego Morales: Yes, it flags regressions against baseline prompt sets and highlights prompts with high hallucination rates. You get per-prompt metrics, token costs, and suggested prompt edits.
[07:44] Sofia Patel: Any concerns about PHI leaving our VPC during evals?
[07:48] Avery Chen: For PII/PHI, we recommend Private or Dedicated with VPC peering and no telemetry collection. If you need us to run evals, anonymize beforehand; we can provide a scrubber and guide.
[07:58] Diego Morales: Ok I'm going to run one more example — showing how guardrails attach. This example will intentionally try to get the model to hallucinate a past diagnosis; the guardrail marks it as unsupported and we map to 'requires human review'.
[08:12] Maya Reed: Nice.
[08:14] [demo response noise]
[08:18] Diego Morales: Output shows a 'flagged' status and an explanation: "no corroborating evidence in patient records". We also log the partial JSON so you can inspect.
[08:30] Liam O'Connor: If we want to integrate with our backlog, can we auto-create tickets?
[08:34] Diego Morales: Yes, function-calling can point to a ticketing webhook; you'll receive the structured payload and can create the ticket. We can demonstrate a sample integration.
[08:42] Avery Chen: Quick pause — any regulatory or legal folks on the call?
[08:46] Sofia Patel: Not on this call, but we'll loop them in for the security review.
[08:50] Avery Chen: Good. We'll send the security docs.
[08:54] [short silence]
[09:00] Diego Morales: Now a few gotchas: JSON mode relies on good schemas; ambiguous schemas lead to variable outputs. Also beware of very large arrays — we recommend page tokens or batched outputs.
[09:14] Maya Reed: For recommended_actions we want up to 5 items, but sometimes the model emits heuristics — can we cap arrays?
[09:20] Diego Morales: Schema can define maxItems, and strict mode enforces it; post-processors can truncate or pad.
[09:26] Liam O'Connor: How do you handle updates to schemas — versioning?
[09:29] Diego Morales: We support schema versioning and pinning per-route. The Console shows diffs when you update a schema and you can do canary rollouts.
[09:38] Maya Reed: That sounds useful.
[09:40] [typing]
[09:44] Diego Morales: Alright, time to summarize and next steps.
[09:48] Avery Chen: Recap: we'll share security pack and sample cost sheet, provide a POC proposal for a 2-week Dedicated slot, and Diego will supply the eval harness script. We'll also schedule a security deep-dive with your legal/compliance.
[09:58] Sofia Patel: Sounds good. For the POC we'll provide 5k anonymized notes by next Tuesday.
[10:04] Liam O'Connor: I'll take the eval script and run locally, then send results.
[10:08] Maya Reed: Can you also share the sample schema and console screenshots?
[10:12] Avery Chen: Yes — links coming.
[10:14] [pause]
[10:18] Sofia Patel: Any final questions?
[10:20] Maya Reed: No, thanks — good demo.
[10:22] Avery Chen: Thanks all.
[10:24] [call ends]
